$comment: Maps named compliance controls to the questions in roadmap.json, and through
them to the test or module that proves each one.
This file names controls and says which questions bear on them. It never
carries a status of its own -- every status in docs/COMPLIANCE.md is derived
from the questions listed here, so a control cannot claim more than the
ledger does. That is the whole design: `mix ash_enterprise.roadmap --check`
fails CI if the rendered page and this file disagree.
Revisions this was written against, 2026-08-19: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria
(2017, revised 2022 points of focus); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A; GDPR
(Regulation (EU) 2016/679). Control identifiers move between revisions -- ISO
renumbered substantially in 2022 -- so going stale is a normal reason to
update this rather than a defect in it.
`criteria` is the ownership contract read by `mix ash_compliance.controls.check`:
one row per SOC 2 criterion saying who owns it, how it is evidenced and what
proves it. A row never carries a status either. Whether a criterion is
evidenced is derived from dated artifacts when it is asked, and the answers
are owned, evidenced or unknown. A reference that does not exist yet is left
out, so the checker reports it; nothing is pointed at a producer or test that

controls.name: Logical access — authorization
controls.asks: Access to data and systems is restricted to authorized users, and the basis of that authorization is defined.
controls.note: The strongest area. Authorization is `(role, privilege, depth)` data evaluated as a pure union with no deny rules, and a conformance suite asserts the resulting truth table rather than a sample of it. The gap is column-level: q6 is partial, with one field policy on one resource, so 'restricted' is still mostly a row-level claim.

controls.name: Registration and authorization of new users
controls.asks: Users are registered and authorized before being issued credentials, and access is removed when no longer required.
controls.note: Registration and deactivation exist as audited, named actions. A deactivated user loses authorization on the next request, but nothing asserts that sign-in or an issued token is refused, and deprovisioning driven by the customer's directory does not exist — q30 is partial, so removal depends on someone here being told.

controls.name: Access is modified and removed on a role change
controls.asks: Access rights are added, modified and removed based on roles, and changes are authorized.
controls.note: A role assignment is an ordinary audited resource, so a grant produces an event naming grantor, grantee and request. Impersonation is attributed but not yet gated (q32).

controls.name: Monitoring — logs are complete and protected
controls.asks: The system is monitored, and log data is protected against alteration.
controls.note: Completeness and protection are answered: audit is inherited rather than wired per resource, and the log is hash-chained with a trigger refusing UPDATE and DELETE. Monitoring is not — q38 is open, and 'logs nobody reads' is the classic finding here.

controls.name: Evaluation of security events
controls.asks: Security events are evaluated to determine whether they represent a failure, and the evaluation is evidenced.
controls.note: The weakest area on the board, and it is a process gap rather than a code one: alerts go nowhere, no rota exists, and nothing records that a human looked.

controls.name: Incident response
controls.asks: Identified incidents are responded to, contained and communicated.
controls.note: The correlation id makes an investigation tractable at 3am — one id reconstructs a whole operation. Nothing makes the investigation start.

controls.name: Change management
controls.asks: Changes to infrastructure, data and software are authorized, designed, tested and approved before implementation.
controls.note: Schema change is the strong half: migrations are derived from resources and `mix ash.codegen --check` fails CI on drift, so a schema cannot diverge from the model unnoticed. Approval of changes to *this* system is CI and review, which is evidence an auditor accepts; approval of changes *within* the product is q24 and is stronger.

controls.name: Access control
controls.asks: Rules for physical and logical access are established based on business and information security requirements.
controls.note: The rules are data, not code — which is what makes them reviewable by someone who does not read Elixir. That is unusually good evidence for this control.

controls.name: Logging
controls.asks: Logs recording activities, exceptions and faults are produced, stored and protected.
controls.note: Produced and protected: yes, with a test that tampers to prove it. Stored: q36 is open — nothing expires and nothing is committed to being kept, so the retention half is satisfied by accident.

controls.name: Monitoring activities
controls.asks: Networks, systems and applications are monitored for anomalous behaviour and appropriate action is taken.
controls.note: Telemetry exists and is exported by OpenTelemetry; anomaly detection and action do not.

controls.name: Use of cryptography
controls.asks: Rules for the effective use of cryptography, including key management, are defined and implemented.
controls.note: Present only where integrity needed it: SHA-256 over the audit chain. Encryption at rest, in transit and key management are the deployment's, and this repository says nothing about them — which is a gap in the map, not a strength.

controls.name: Right of access
controls.asks: A data subject can obtain confirmation of processing and a copy of their data.
controls.note: For audit data, yes and per tenant. For the subject's own records there is no assembled export — q19 is planned, and a data inventory is the prerequisite.

controls.name: Right to erasure
controls.asks: A data subject can obtain erasure of their personal data without undue delay.
controls.note: The sharpest conflict in the repository, and it got sharper deliberately: soft delete means a destroy is reversible by design, and the audit log now actively refuses DELETE. ADR 0024 resolves it by crypto-shredding rather than by weakening either. Its erasure half is built (2026-10-12): content from an external connection is sealed under that connection's key, and destroying the key reaches the audit log without breaking the chain. Per-person erasure is partial (q14: names and emails in canonical_people survive a shred) and partitioning is not built (q36), so the control stays open and says so.

controls.name: Records of processing activities
controls.asks: A controller maintains a record of processing activities, including categories of data and recipients.
controls.note: Every processing *event* is recorded in detail; the *register* of activities, categories and recipients is not. q39 is open, and a sub-processor list is the first thing a customer's privacy team asks for.

controls.name: Security of processing
controls.asks: Appropriate technical measures ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience.
controls.note: Confidentiality and integrity are the strong half — tenant isolation is tested to hold even when authorization is wrong, and the log is verifiably intact. Availability and resilience are untested: q48 is open, and an untested restore is a belief rather than a measure.

criteria.rationale: The adopting organization's code of conduct and its acknowledgement. Software here holds neither.
Board or committee oversight is the adopting organization's. No process is defined here.
Reporting lines are the adopting organization's. The platform models business units, positions and managers as data used for authorization, not as the organization's chart of record.
Hiring, training and retention are people processes outside the platform.
Accountability for control duties is assigned by the adopting organization.
The audit export hands a reviewer a window of the log with the chain hashes. Nothing schedules it or records the result as an artifact.
Internal communication of control duties is a policy and training process. None is defined here.
Communication with customers and outside parties is the adopting organization's.
Objective setting is the adopting organization's.
The risk register and its review are the adopting organization's. No register or review process exists in this repository.
Fraud risk assessment is a review process. None is defined here.
Assessing significant changes for control impact is a review process. None is defined here.
Separate evaluation of the audit log: the verify task walks every chain and the suite tampers on purpose. CI evaluates the rest on each push. Nothing schedules the verify task or stores its result.
Deficiency tracking is meant to be the findings the ownership sweep raises. This host does not schedule the sweep, so no producer is named.
Selecting control activities against risk is a review process. None is defined here.
Every resource inherits tenancy, ownership, audit and the policy union from the platform base resource, and the conformance suite asserts the truth table of the grants.
Policies and procedures, and the record that people read them, are outside the platform. The platform has nothing that publishes or acknowledges a policy.
Authorization is (role, privilege, depth) data evaluated as a pure union of grants. Column-level restriction is open (q6).

Access requests are recorded and decided by a process. A deactivated user loses authorization on the next request (conformance suite), but no test asserts that sign-in or an issued token is refused (q30), and no quarterly review of who holds access is defined here.
Role assignments are audited resources that name the grantor and the grantee. Impersonation is attributed but not gated (q32).
Physical access to the hosting facility belongs to the hosting provider. This repository names no provider and holds no provider report.

Data disposal is crypto-shredding: destroying a key makes sealed content unreadable. Per-person erasure is partial (q14), retention-driven disposal of the audit log is not built (q36), and media disposal belongs to the hosting provider.
Network boundary, firewall and edge protection are the deployment's. This repository has no infrastructure code.
force_ssl is set for production in config/prod.exs. No test asserts it and transit protection beyond the application is the deployment's.
CI runs a security scan of the web code and an audit of dependencies. Neither detects malware on hosts, which is the deployment's.
CI scans code and audits dependencies on each push. CI has no schedule and the repository configures no dependency update service, so a vulnerability published after the last push is not seen.
Log completeness and tamper evidence are carried: the log is hash-chained and a trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE. Review of the logs and alerting are not (q38).
Evaluating events to decide whether they are incidents needs people and a rota. Neither exists here (q49).
Incident response needs a plan, a rota and customer communication. None is defined here (q49).
Recovery from incidents needs a plan and a tested restore. Neither is defined here (q48).
CI gates every change: format, compile with warnings as errors, credo, schema drift, tests. Whether review and approval are required before merge is a repository setting, not code here.
Business disruption risk mitigation is the adopting organization's.
Vendor risk review is a process over the adopting organization's vendor register. None is defined here.
Capacity monitoring is the deployment's. Telemetry exports to a collector when configured and no target or alert exists (q28, q47).
Backup and recovery infrastructure is the deployment's. This repository configures none (q48).
Testing recovery plans needs a plan and a restore drill. Neither exists here (q48).
Processing specifications are declared on resources: actions, state machines and policies, and schema drift fails CI.
Input checks are the validations and constraints each host declares on its own actions. The platform supplies the mechanism.
An illegal state transition is rejected: each transition is a named action and there is no generic update that sets a state.
Output checks are specific to each host's reports and exports.
Stored audit items are tamper-evident. Other stored items are protected by soft delete and tenant isolation, not by integrity checks.
Protection is carried: tenant isolation and redaction of sensitive values from the log. Identifying what is confidential needs a data inventory, which is open (q39).
Same mechanism as CC6.5: crypto-shredding. Retention-driven disposal is not built (q36).
The privacy notice is the adopting organization's.
Choice and consent capture is a product behaviour of each host. The platform records a tenant's sub-processor opt-in and has no end-user consent model.
Stating purposes of collection is the adopting organization's. The data inventory is open (q39).
Explicit consent for sensitive personal information is a product behaviour of each host.
Use limited to stated purposes is a policy each host enforces. The platform limits disclosure to model sub-processors (see P6.1) and nothing wider.
Retention of personal information has no policy or job for the audit log (q36). Lineage records are pruned after 14 days, which is a different record.
Crypto-shredding covers content that arrives through a connection. People and core platform resources are not sealed, so per-person erasure is partial (q14).
A subject's own records have no assembled export (q19). The audit export covers audit data per tenant only.
Correction of personal information is an ordinary update action in each host. No request process is defined here.
Disclosure to a model sub-processor is refused unless the tenant has recorded an opt-in, and every unknown case is a refusal. Other disclosures are not covered.
Authorized disclosures to model sub-processors are recorded in the judgment ledger when the instrument is in-zone. A register of other disclosures does not exist (q39).
Recording unauthorized disclosures is an incident process. None is defined here (q49).
Holding third parties to privacy commitments needs signed agreements. This repository holds none.
Third-party incident reporting is a contractual term. This repository holds none.
Breach notification is an incident process. None is defined here (q49).
Accounting of disclosures needs a register of sub-processors and disclosures (q39), which does not exist.
Accuracy and completeness are data-quality rules each host declares. The platform ships master data quality rules as an example, not as a control.
Complaint handling and monitoring of privacy compliance are the adopting organization's.
